items.body: In other states, even conservative strongholds like Kansas , voters have upheld abortion rights. But the abortion debate is not in Kansas anymore. Now it’s in Idaho. And it’s open warfare. Supporters and opponents have raised $9.7 million — so far — in the campaign over Proposition 1, a voter initiative to rescind Idaho’s near-complete abortion ban. Proposition 1 is by far the biggest political battle in the state, and, sensing opportunity, everyone wants a piece of the action. “Both sides are working to mobilize people to vote on that issue,” said Jaclyn Kettler, a political science professor at Boise State University. Proposition 1, explained For a quick and useful overview of what Proposition 1 would do, here’s a summary from Idaho Capital Sun . That also makes Proposition 1 a wild card. The hottest item on the ballot could drive turnout in other Nov. 3 elections — such as the governor’s and the state superintendent’s races; legislative races in Idaho’s scattered swing districts; and the $307 million in school levy requests . The high-powered opposition But for now, let’s focus on Proposition 1 itself. The parochial and partisan opposition is impossible to ignore. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has contributed $1 million in opposition to Proposition 1 . The Catholic Diocese of Boise has contributed $300,000 . The Idaho Republican Party, meanwhile, has gone all-in against Proposition 1. State GOP chairwoman Dorothy Moon has made the initiative nearly a staple of the weekly op-ed she sends to news outlets; six of her last 10 op-eds mentioned Proposition 1 in whole or in part. Last week, the GOP rolled out a news release touting near unanimous opposition to Proposition 1, from statewide elected officials and Idaho’s congressional delegation. “If there is one issue that unites Republicans across the ideological spectrum, it is that of life,” Moon said. (The only name not on the list: Secretary of State Phil McGrane. Asked about it Tuesday, Moon deferred to McGrane, who did not respond to messages from EdNews.) For many Republicans, the Proposition 1 fight is more than just a little personal. After all, the initiative challenges abortion restrictions passed by an overwhelmingly Republican Legislature — and signed into law by Gov. Brad Little, who is seeking a third term next month. Little last week voiced his opposition to Proposition 1, saying it would “make abortion far more accessible in Idaho.” For the state’s prevailing party — and for two of the state’s largest religious groups — fighting Proposition 1 is a matter of seeking to protect the status quo. That alone is a driver, possibly the main one. The down-ticket implications: two recent examples The Republicans’ campaign against Proposition 1 is a marked departure from 2018. And it echoes 2024. Let’s look more closely at both of those elections. In 2018, the Idaho GOP was virtually silent on the Reclaim Idaho Medicaid expansion initiative. In essence, the Idaho Freedom Foundation led the opposition to Medicaid expansion. Buoyed by a broad coalition of support, the initiative passed easily. Down ticket, Democrats picked up four legislative seats. In 2024, the GOP and Republican leaders went all-in to fight Reclaim Idaho’s ranked-choice voting initiative. Ranked choice went down in flames, receiving just 30% support. Down ticket, Republicans added three legislative seats. A lot of variables shape election results. After all, 2024 was a presidential election year, and it proved to be a big night for the GOP, in Idaho and nationally. Meanwhile, 2018 was a midterm election, and those tend to be at least slightly more favorable to Idaho Democrats. In other words, the 2018 and 2024 flips in the Legislature could have been caused by any number of other factors. Which brings us to 2026. He also said there are multiple ways for a voter to prove identification and residency, and an Idaho judge has ruled the state’s voting laws are constitutional. The groups, Babe Vote and the League of Women Voters of Idaho , say Idaho’s identification and proof of residency requirements create barriers to voting that affect students and older voters alike. Olivia Luna, a 21-year-old Idaho college student and Babe Vote leader, said a pair of 2023 state laws that removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification for voting hurt students and young people especially hard. House Bill 124 removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification for voting. House Bill 340 also removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification and standardized voter registration requirements for in-person registration and online registration. House Bill 340 also required the Idaho Transportation Department to create and offer no-fee identification cards that are accepted for voting. Luna said many students frequently move between their parents’ house, dorms and apartments throughout their academic career, making it difficult to prove residency from a list of documents accepted by the state. Luna said Babe Vote paused its voter registration efforts after the laws took effect, and the laws continue to make Babe Vote’s voter registration and outreach efforts difficult. Luna said she appreciates the opportunities to work with McGrane’s office. items.body: Jeremey Varley, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture's southern chief treatment engineer, explains the state's strategy for eradicating invasive quagga mussels during a boat tour of the infested portion of the Snake River on Oct. 3, 2025. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt told a committee of state legislators Tuesday that she believes Idaho’s population of invasive quagga mussels is very small and confined to limited sections of the Snake River. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE In September 2023, state officials used water sampling to c onfirm the presence of quagga mussel larvae for the first time in state history. During water sampling this year, state officials found eight veliger mussels, the larvae form of the mussels, Tewalt said during a meeting of the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Committee at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. Scuba divers also found what Tewalt described as “a number of adult mussels” while searching the Snake River. The mussels, which were discovered in the Snake River near Twin Falls, can reproduce extremely rapidly, clog pipes and cover boat hulls. If left unchecked, Tewalt said the spread of quagga mussels poses serious threats to the state’s drinking and irrigation water, recreation industry, state budget and economy. Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US In an effort to completely eradicate all of the invasive species, officials with the Idaho State Department of Agriculture have been administering lethal copper chemicals into the affected part of the Snake River each year since the mussels were first detected. Compared to previous years, the amount of mussels discovered in water sampling is lower and the affected section of the Snake River is smaller this year, Tewalt told legislators. “What it would signify is a very small population,” Tewalt said. After detecting the mussels again this summer, the ag department moved forward with another round of copper-based treatments – with scuba divers injecting the chemicals in harder to reach nooks, crannies and fissures in rock. Chanel Tewalt serves as the director of the Idaho Department of Agriculture. (Courtesy of Idaho State Department of Agriculture) “Copper in the water means that reproduction cycle (for the mussels) is halted,” Tewalt said. Along with mussels, the copper also kills fish and other aquatic life in the river. This year, Tewalt said there have been fewer fish killed and that state officials are not stocking the sections of the river being treated with copper with new fish. Although the mussels were first discovered in water samples in 2023, Tewalt told legislators the mussels have likely been in the Twin Falls pool of the Snake River for longer. Water sampling and monitoring for quagga mussels is an ongoing, years-long process. items.body: Boise State University athletics has the green light to go $18 million in the red. With some reluctance, the State Board of Education approved the deficit spending plan Wednesday afternoon. Most of the $18 million will go into “revenue sharing” — direct payments to student-athletes. And Boise State will use a variety of budget reserves to cover the $18 million. “I personally don’t even like the term … deficit in athletics,” Boise State President David Hahn told State Board members. “Boise State is not running a deficit. We are managing our reserves, we are managing our finances. I’m putting that capital where it needs to be for success of all of the missions.” The $18 million figure is not necessarily unexpected. In August, Boise State Athletic Director Jeramiah Dickey warned the State Board that the cost of revenue sharing — and expenses tied to a move from the Mountain West Conference to a reformed Pac-12 conference — would drive the program into the red. Wednesday’s meeting brought the budget picture into more focus. Boise State is now projecting a $16.9 million deficit for the current budget year, which ends June 30. In August, Dickey pegged this year’s deficit at $14 million to $18 million. The university will provide the athletic department $3 million for debt service. The athletic department hopes to clear $2 million from special events at Albertsons Stadium. The stadium hosted two nights of the Banana Ball baseball barnstorming tour on July 31 and Aug. 1, and country singer Luke Combs is scheduled to perform at Albertsons Stadium on June 12, at the tail end of the budget year. Revenue sharing will increase to about $14.1 million, up from about $10 million. Colleges and universities can spend up to $21.6 million in revenue sharing, and the Boise State payments tie into “overall competitiveness” with rival programs, Dickey told board members. One unknown is the revenue Boise State will collect from the new-look Pac-12, now in its inaugural season. In time, Boise State expects to reap increased revenues from its new conference. But for this year, the university is budgeting for flat conference revenues, unchanged from its final season in the Mountain West, said Stacy Pearson, Boise State’s interim CFO. If the deficit exceeds $18 million, Boise State athletics would have to come back to the State Board for additional spending authority. The State Board approved the deficit spending plan unanimously, but not without discussion. Board member Shawn Keough — a former state senator who co-chaired the Legislature’s budget-writing Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee — said she was “really uncomfortable” with the vote. “I really don’t want to be here in a couple months or another year. Something has to give.” Board President Kurt Liebich said the deficit spending gives Boise State the flexibility it needs during a time of turmoil in college sports. The Senate has passed a college sports overhaul bill , but it is on hold in the House. “(We’re) giving you all the runway you need to figure it out, and I think you guys deserve that runway because of the sustained success you’ve had for 30 years,” said Liebich, who sits on a gubernatorial working group that has been studying the future of Idaho college athletics. Board member David Turnbull described Wednesday’s vote in stark terms. “The option is to basically put a bullet in Bronco sports if we don’t give them this runway.” The State Board is meeting at Lewis-Clark State College through Thursday.

items.body: Some legislative districts have elder statesmen who have been in office for years. But that’s no longer the case in District 25, encompassing the city of Twin Falls. It’s the only district this November with no incumbents on the ballot. Republican primary voters in May ousted two freshman lawmakers, and seven-term Republican Rep. Lance Clow resigned in late 2025. Republican candidate Casey Swensen, who defeated Sen. Josh Kohl in the primary, said the three newcomers from District 25 will face a steep learning curve in writing legislation, understanding bills and working with other lawmakers in Boise. “There’s a lot of seniority-based stuff up there, so we’re going to have to work as a coalition to be effective,” Swensen said. It’s a reliably Republican district. Democrat Lane Startin’s 2024 campaign against Clow was the first time a Democrat was on the ballot in Twin Falls since 2018. He took 28% of the vote. Startin now faces Swensen in the general election. “It’s a tall order, but you just got to keep swinging at it,” Startin said of his chances on Nov. 3. items.summary: Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador addresses attendees during the Idaho National Guard's Cyber Discovery 2026 conference at the state's Chinden campus in Boise on June 9, 2026. Rusty Rehl/U.S. Army National Guard) Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador on Wednesday joined seven other states in announcing separate lawsuits against OpenAI, alleging the company’s chatbot ChatGPT harm.
items.body: Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador addresses attendees during the Idaho National Guard's Cyber Discovery 2026 conference at the state's Chinden campus in Boise on June 9, 2026. (Photo by Sgt. Rusty Rehl/U.S. Army National Guard) Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador on Wednesday joined seven other states in announcing separate lawsuits against OpenAI, alleging the company’s chatbot ChatGPT harm. The 107-page lawsui t filed in Ada County Fourth Judicial District Court alleges that the company has harmed Idaho children and deceived adults in violation of the Idaho Consumer Protection Act . “We have watched technology giants experience tremendous growth and gains while putting consumers, especially children, at significant risk,” Labrador said in a press release. “The safety of Idaho’s children cannot be an afterthought to runaway profit or technological advancements. We will hold OpenAI accountable for their reckless priorities.” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email that the company continues to improve its safeguards and respond to “misalignment.” “We’ve built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack,” Pusateri wrote. “While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.” Attorneys general in Arkansas, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia, Iowa, Kansas and Arizona filed similar lawsuits in their state courts Wednesday, Reuters reported. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE What’s in Idaho’s OpenAI lawsuit? Labrador, deputy attorneys general Matthew Maurer and Stephanie Guyon, and private attorneys from the Los Angeles and New York City offices of Kibler Fowler & Cave LLP brought Idaho’s lawsuit. The complaint alleges that OpenAI misled the public “into believing that OpenAI is a responsible actor and that ChatGPT was and is a safe, teen-appropriate tool that puts safety first.” “Designed to be overly agreeable and feign human compassion, ChatGPT has proven that it can be incredibly dangerous to vulnerable users, like children, and the public,” the lawsuit states. The attorneys argue the company falsely represented the safety, reliability and accuracy of ChatCPT. It also argues the company failed to disclose personal data was collected from children under 13, and failed to warn users of risk of self-harm, violence and suicide. “Given these accelerating threats, Attorney General Labrador is suing to compel OpenAI’s compliance with the Idaho Consumer Protection Act and to cease its dangerous activities that have put Idahoans in harm’s way with willfully reckless and unlawful conduct,” the press release said. The state’s attorneys are asking the court to declare OpenAI violated Idaho law, order the company to pay $5,000 to the state for each violation of the law, and pay actual damages and restitution. The complaint also asks the court to stop the company from testing advanced AI models “outside of a secured, independently verified testing environment,” and to require the company to adopt additional safety measures and protocols. The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior auth
items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A panel of Idaho lawmakers that studied issues in the health insurance market on Wednesday formalized plans to develop legislation to address a range of issues that affect access to health care. The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior authorization, a cost-control measure that health insurers use to deny covering certain treatments, and to target several other issues that the interim legislative committee heard about in its meetings in the last few months and through surveys it sent to insurers and health care providers. In a series of votes, the interim committee teed up a series of bills focused on health insurance that could be considered by the Legislature when it returns next January. Some of the other bills that could be drafted could address: Reducing delayed payments to providers, by setting standards for providers and insurers; Establishing uniform standards to credential health care providers through insurers; and Requiring the Idaho Department of Insurance, which regulates health insurers, to collect and present to the Legislature data about the timeliness of payments, and healthcare denial rates. That might also include information on one arbitration tool created by Congress that the state’s largest insurer, Blue Cross of Idaho, claims that a North Idaho microhospital heavily relies upon. Blue Cross argues the practice could drive up the cost of healthcare , and Congress is considering overhauling the tool. The potential prior authorization reform bill wouldn’t be the Legislature’s first attempt to address the issue, which some patients say can delay access to healthcare through drawn out timelines to issue decisions. Earlier this year, a bill, House Bill 611 , set out to require more transparency and establish timelines in the process, but it never received a committee hearing. Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, listens to proceedings during the Jan. 12, 2026, Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Prior authorization also impacts healthcare providers. Providers in Idaho reported spending more time on administrative work to respond to prior authorization requests in recent years, according to data that committee co-chairman Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, summarized. In 2025, an American Medical Association survey found that 92% of physicians reported negative patient impacts caused by prior authorization processes. The committee was formed after a now-resolved contract fallout between a hospital in East Idaho, Portneuf Medical Center, and the insurer that runs the health plan for state employees, Regence BlueShield of Idaho. In the coming years, the state plans to transition Medicaid, a health insurance public assistance program for people who have disabilities or earn low-incomes, from being state-run to being managed by private health insurance companies . items.title: Pocatello trustees lean toward keeping five-day week
items.summary: Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees appear inclined to keep the district’s five-day school week after discussing the matter during a board work session Tuesday. The board will vote next week to either stay on a five-day schedule or move to four-day model. The board will also consider swapping the current trimester schedule for semesters. The district began considering these and other changes in June. Four
items.body: Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees appear inclined to keep the district’s five-day school week after discussing the matter during a board work session Tuesday. The board will vote next week to either stay on a five-day schedule or move to four-day model. The board will also consider swapping the current trimester schedule for semesters. The district began considering these and other changes in June. Four-day weeks have gained popularity across Idaho in recent years. Last school year, about two in three districts used four-day calendars. Eighteen of the state’s 76 charter schools use the model. In 2024, Nampa — similar in size to Pocatello-Chubbuck — became Idaho’s largest district to join the trend, which is most common among smaller districts. Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees favor five-day week Trustees Heather Clarke, Megan Furniss, Deanna Judy and Bill Osborn said they would vote to maintain the five-day week in Pocatello because of concerns a four-day week would negatively impact learning and be a difficult change for staff. Furniss pointed to families who rely on the district’s social services. Only a quarter of families with children who qualify for free and reduced-price lunch responded to a recent four-day week survey, she said, creating a “gaping hole” in the results. A survey of parents and district employees with 2,700 respondents found a split in community opinion: 56%, or about 1,500 respondents, said a four-day week is ideal. “In the end, public education is intended to serve every student,” not just families who can arrange childcare on Fridays, Furniss said. Osborn pointed to numbers showing that just 2% of schools nationwide are on a four-day week, convincing him that the five-day week is better. Judy called a switch “a huge jump.” She spoke about a hybrid model where students attend school two Fridays a month, but Clarke repeatedly objected, saying it wasn’t the purpose of the workshop. Meanwhile, Clarke, Furniss and Board Chair Raymond Knoff said they prefer the district’s current trimester system over semesters. Furniss cited students’ abilities to take more electives in an academic year. The board will also vote on the trimester-semester option next week. Other business Trustees also discussed a survey of more than 2,000 Pocatello-Chubbuck high school students regarding their preferred career-technical education (CTE) offerings. Culinary arts, welding and health professions were the most popular among students. Seventy-eight percent of students said it is important that their electives connect to future career pathways. Much of trustees’ discussion centered on military science, one of the least popular options on the survey. Pocatello Director of Business Jonathan Balls also presented the board with a summary of completed facilities maintenance projects, including an update on the Highland High School rebuild project. The school caught fire and saw severe damage in 2023.

(Photo illustration by Getty Images) The political action committee opposing Idaho’s Proposition 1 abortion rights initiative collected nearly $1.5 million since the end of September, buoyed by two large donations from churches. The Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, reported the previously announced $1 million donation from the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on Oct. 8. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise donated another $300,000 to the PAC opposing the initiative the next day. Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions Since Sept. 29, Too Extreme for Idaho received $153,985 from 32 individual people and $1.3 million from four organizations, including the two churches. Too Extreme for Idaho has raised a total of just over $4 million, campaign finance data shows. As of Monday, the PAC supporting the initiative, Idahoans United for Women and Families, brought in more than $630,000 since Sept. 29. The largest donation came from the federal Government that Works PAC, based out of Washington, D.C, which gave $250,000. Oklahoma-based billionaire philanthropist Lynn Schusterman donated $200,000 on Sept. 30, campaign finance data shows. Since Sept. 29, the PAC received $265,290 from 81 individuals and $370,000 from three organizations. In total, Idahoans United has collected more than $5.6 million. Independent expenditures for and against Prop 1 total more than $2.5 million Groups and individuals spent more than $2.5 million combined to support and oppose Prop 1 in independent expenditures, which includes spending by organizations or individuals spent directly to support or oppose a ballot measure. items.body: The Idaho Department of Lands managed the Tyson Fire, which firefighters responded to in Benewah County in July 2023. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands) More than 80% of the wildfires that the Idaho Department of Lands has responded to this year have been caused by humans, Director Dustin Miller told an interim committee of Idaho legislators Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “This staggering figure just underscores the importance of not only a robust fuels mitigation program … but also a solid prevention program,” Miller told the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Interim Committee during a meeting at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. Through the end of September, a total of 10,000 acres of land that the Idaho Department of Lands is responsible for protecting has burned. (That figure does not include the larger number of acres of federal land, such as U.S. Forest Service land, that burned in wildfires this summer.) Dustin Miller is the director of the Idaho Department of Lands. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands) The increase in human-caused fires is not new. In 2023, Miller also told a commission of statewide elected officials that he was investigating a spike in human-caused fires , the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Miller told state legislators the costs of wildfires are high, and several legislators immediately pushed for more answers. Through the end of September, the state’s wildfire costs were a little over $47 million, of which an estimated $19.8 million could be reimbursable from other agencies the state partners with, Miller said. In addition to the financial cost to taxpayers, fires also can also threaten the safety of firefighters and the public, destroy property and burn state endowment timber lands that generate funding for public schools and other beneficiaries. There is also the cost of rehabilitation and recovery following fire and the long-term effects caused by fire. Idaho legislators ask how state can recoup costs for human-caused fires While human-caused fires aren’t new, the 80% figure grabbed the attention of several legislators. Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, asked Miller if the state was doing enough to go after the people who were responsible. Natural Resources Interim Committee Co-Chair Britt Raybould, R-Rexburg, asked if stronger penalties would be a deterrent. “Just something that encourages people to think a little more responsibly about how their behavior can have, not only the financial, but the environmental and property damage and all of the surrounding consequences,” Raybould said. State Rep. Britt Raybould, R-Rexburg, speaks from the floor of the Idaho House of Representatives on March 16, 2026, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Miller told the committee that the state investigates the cause of every fire and attempts to recoup funding from individuals or groups that are deemed “negligent.” Sometimes the recovery process works well, Miller said, but sometimes it can take years to recover the money, and the state doesn’t always succeed. “Oftentimes we settle for less than what the suppression costs were,” Miller said. “We really try to work with the individual and their insurance companies,” Miller added. “These are taxpayers always, and we want to recoup as much as we can back to the general taxpayer. But you know, we have been fairly successful.” During a break in Tuesday’s meeting, Miller told the Sun the causes of the fires include people losing control of their burning debris piles, sparks caused by chains or other metal equipment, discarded cigarette butts, escaped camp fires that were never fully extinguished and more. The Boise School District is launching an internal investigation into reported online death threats against a student. Details on the district’s Timberline High School investigation are unclear. “We cannot disclose individual student discipline due to student privacy requirements,” district spokesman Dan Hollar said in an email to Idaho EdNews. The district had put its investigation on hold while waiting on the Boise Police Department. Police finished their interviews Wednesday, “and we were … given the all clear to begin investigating on our own,” Boise district Area Director Shelley Bonds told the Boise School Board Monday evening. The Boise police investigation is ongoing, spokeswoman Haley Kramer told EdNews Tuesday morning. “We have completed the initial essential interviews, preserved immediately available evidence, and requested preservation of additional evidence not yet received.” Police were brought in on the investigation on Oct. 2, the day the threats were reported to school and district officials. According to an online petition, members of the Timberline football team went on the Snapchat social media site and talked about raping and killing a female student. Boise police increased their presence at the school last week. District and school officials postponed some homecoming activities and canceled a homecoming football game scheduled for Thursday , citing concerns about student safety. Hundreds of Timberline students staged a walkout during classes Wednesday . Students demonstrate in front of Timberline High in Boise on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More As the 2026 Nov. 3 general election approaches, Idahoans have been asking questions about filling out ballots, write-in candidates, online voter registration searches, and more as they gear up to vote. The Idaho Capital Sun spoke to Secretary of State Phil McGrane and his staff about some of the top concerns that have arisen this election season. Here are some of the most frequently asked questions: If I don’t fill in a response to every question, does my ballot still count? Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane attends the State of the State Address at the State Capitol building in Boise on Jan. 8, 2024. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Voters can skip any question or race on their ballot if they choose to. McGrane had heard concerns from voters worried that if they didn’t fill out a response to one of the ballot questions, that the rest of their ballot would be thrown out. This won’t happen, he said. “Voters are not required to vote in every race on their ballot for it to count,” the secretary of state’s office spokesperson Joe Parris said in an email. “If they skip a question or contest, the remaining selections on their ballot will still be counted.” Can I write in a candidate or write in an answer to the state gun advisory question? Prospective write-in candidates in Idaho must file a “Declaration of Intent” to run with the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office, and the deadline to do so was Sept. 4. Voters may still write in a name, but that vote won’t count if it doesn’t go toward a registered write-in candidate. This year, the only write-in candidate who filed this declaration is independent gubernatorial candidate Jacob Burnett, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. For House Joint Resolution 4 , House Joint Resolution 6 , and Proposition 1 , there are only “yes” or “no” options to fill out on the ballot. The advisory question about selecting an official state gun has six choices of gun and no option to write in a response. Are signatures on absentee ballots verified, and how? Signatures on all absentee ballots are verified, Idaho Secretary of State’s Office officials said. Election staff members compare signatures on the ballots with voter registration, signature history on previous ballots, and driver’s license records to confirm a match before ballots are counted, Parris said. “Make sure you sign your own absentee ballot,” Parris said. “A common mistake is a spouse putting their return ballot in the wrong return ballot envelope.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. A candidate forum for those seeking a position for the Ada County Highway District will be from 7-8:30 p.m. Oct 27 at Boise’s South Junior High School, 3101 W. Cassia St. Candidates who have confirmed attendance include Sean Sundwall and Miranda Gold for District 3, as well as Marisa Keith, Dave Case and Chris Campbell for District 4. The forum is sponsored by League of Women Voters of Idaho and the American Association of University Women. “Sadly, the number of opportunities Idaho voters have to interact directly with candidates from across the political spectrum is shrinking,” said Jean Henscheid, League of Women Voters of Idaho president. “We applaud those who have stepped up to meet with each other and with the voting public to engage in this critical aspect of the democratic process. The Federal Election Commission’s criteria for non-debates will be applied to both forums. A moderator will ask each candidate questions written by audience members. The moderator may interject clarifying questions, and a timekeeper will ensure that each candidate receives equal opportunities to speak. items.body: All three candidates for Idaho’s top education job say that the state should be more transparent about who’s benefiting from a fledgling private school choice program. Incumbent state superintendent Debbie Critchfield, a Republican, faced challengers Becky Sundin Mitchell, a Democrat, and Teresa Roundy of the Constitution Party in a live, televised debate Monday. Idaho News 6, a Boise-based TV station, hosted the debate. The candidates agreed on many topics during the hourlong event, including whether the state should release data that shows how many recipients of the Parental Choice Tax Credit were previously enrolled in private school. They also agreed that private schools receiving taxpayer funds should be subject to similar academic reporting requirements as public schools. “It’s no different than any other government program that is funded through taxpayer dollars,” Critchfield said. “We have an expectation to know where those dollars go.” Critchfield added that the state should find out whether parents are satisfied with the education choices that they made for their children. The tax credit offers families up to $5,000 — or $7,500 if they have a disability — to offset private school tuition and other nonpublic education expenses, including homeschooling costs. Since the program launched Jan. 15, the Idaho State Tax Commission, the state agency responsible for administering the tax credit, has yet to release data that would test a key selling point of the program: that it would help students who couldn’t otherwise afford private education. “Any time that taxpayer money is used for anything, there should be accountability attached to it,” Sundin Mitchell said. “I’m concerned that we passed this tax credit system without having any accountability measures in place.” Roundy agreed. “The state should track and publicly report these figures to ensure total transparency, fiscal responsibility and equity for Idaho taxpayers,” she said. “Public funds must be used effectively and should never subsidize the wealthy at the expense of families who are genuinely struggling.” Idaho News 6 senior reporter Riley Shoemaker and neighborhood reporters Greenlee Clark and Allie Triepke moderated the debate. Candidates were given one minute to respond to each question. The candidates also discussed Idaho’s aging school funding formula, school security, facilities funding and special education, among other topics. Click here to watch the full debate. items.body: Idaho’s colleges and universities are seeking more than $170 million for capital projects — requests likely to far outstrip available funding. The money would come from the Permanent Building Fund, which receives a share of lottery dividends and collects a host of tax carveouts. The fund pays for public works projects across state government, not just on campuses. This year’s Permanent Building Fund budget came to $72.5 million. Gov. Brad Little and the Legislature cut into this budget, siphoning $48.5 million in interest earnings into a cash-strapped state general fund budget. Consequently, the state funded only $890,000 for a single capital project this year, an Idaho National Guard request. State agencies requested $229.4 million for capital requests, and most were unfunded. Nonetheless, when Idaho college and university leaders appeared before the Permanent Building Fund’s advisory council Tuesday, they took turns pitching a long list of capital projects. Here’s a closer look at the higher education requests: College of Western Idaho . The state’s largest two-year college has the longest and costliest wish list in the higher education system. items.body: The Professional Standards Commission approved disciplinary actions for five Idaho educators earlier this month. The state commission oversees educator certification and investigates potential violations of Idaho’s educator ethics code. It can impose discipline on an educator’s certificate, including suspension or revocation. Here’s a closer look at the latest disciplinary actions and the educators involved. Revocations Wesley Naylor , Richfield School District Ethics violations: Not maintaining a professional relationship with students Disciplinary action: Certificate revoked In September 2025, Naylor grabbed a student’s arm and/or pushed them as they tried to walk out of the classroom after the student ignored Naylor. Naylor pleaded guilty to disturbing the peace related to the incident in December 2025. Casey Hood , Arizona Ethics violations: Failing to exemplify honesty and integrity in the course of professional practice Disciplinary action: Certificate revoked Hood surrendered her Arizona teaching certificate for five years starting in September 2025 after allegations that she modified expired individualized education plans to make it appear that required meetings had occurred when they had not. Note: Educators listed without a school district were likely not working at an Idaho school when their ethics violations occurred, though they either held or applied for an Idaho certification at some point. Suspension Michael Robert Driscoll, Boise Ethics violations: Failure to refrain from the abuse of alcohol or drugs during the course of professional practice Disciplinary action: Suspension of certificate until completion of an alcohol recovery program In August 2025, a fellow staff member reported that Driscoll smelled like alcohol and had a cup in his classroom with a liquid that also smelled like alcohol. Driscoll was removed from the classroom. He refused an alcohol test, but the liquid in the cup tested positive for alcohol. Driscoll agreed to the disciplinary action, which requires him to complete an alcohol recovery program to get his license reinstated. Letters of reprimand Jessica Bailey, St. Maries Ethics violations: Failed to maintain a professional relationship with students Disciplinary action: Letter of reprimand and completion of an approved-boundaries course Bailey was accused of crossing professional boundaries with a student by being alone with one of them in a classroom without an educational purpose. She exchanged texts with a student that were unrelated to school instruction or responsibilities, including plans to spend time together doing recreational activities and for the student to help with a project at Bailey’s home. Bailey agreed to the disciplinary action. Cheryl Griebenow, Caldwell Ethics violations: Did not fulfill all terms and obligations detailed in the contract with the local school board of education or education agency for the duration of the contract. Disciplinary action: Letter of reprimand Griebenow submitted a letter of resignation in November 2025, which the board of trustees did not accept the following month. Because she was not released from her contract, Griebenow was found to be in violation of the code of ethics. Griebenow agreed to the disciplinary action.

items.body: Boise State University officials on Friday cut the ribbon on the new ESI Construction Management facility, built to serve one of the university’s fastest-growing programs. It’s not just a building, said Anthony Perrenoud, the program’s department chair. It’s a tool for learning. Many of the building’s features are interactive, helping students learn how to assemble a structure. Growth in the Construction Management program was also a factor. “When we designed this building, there were 300 students” in the program, Perrenoud said. Now, it has 560 students. Inside the building The ESI Construction Management building stands out on campus for its extensive use of wood. Wood products company Boise Cascade donated the timber for the project, which is the first mass-timber building on campus. The facility includes student workspaces, a computer lab, classrooms and conference rooms. It also has a 3,300-square-foot “high bay” — a giant garage — with an overhead crane and an outdoor learning area. items.body: Voters cast their ballot for the primary election on May 19, 2026, at Club Apple in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A longtime state performance evaluator is running against Idaho’s longest currently serving statewide elected official in the 2026 general election for Idaho state controller. 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More Democratic candidate Rakesh Mohan is challenging incumbent Republican State Controller Brandon Woolf, who has served as state controller since being appointed in 2012. The state controller is a constitutional officer that serves as Idaho’s chief fiscal officer and serves on the Idaho State Board of Land Commissioners, which is commonly referred to as the Land Board. The position is for a four-year term and comes with an annual salary of $128,690. Meet Democratic challenger Rakesh Mohan Mohan worked as a government auditor and evaluator for 36 years, working for state legislatures in Idaho, Washington, Louisiana and Kansas. He spent the last 21 years of his evaluation career as director of the nonpartisan Idaho Office of Performance Evaluations until he retired in June 2024 . After that, Mohan served as a visiting professor at the School of Public Policy at Boise State University. Mohan is not an accountant or IT professional, but he said his 30-plus years of experience evaluating and auditing government policy and programs has prepared him to serve as controller. He said he is running because he believes in accountability and transparency and did not want to see Woolf run unopposed, like Woolf did in the 2014 and 2018 general elections. “Since I decided to run and I started talking to people, the very first questions I get asked are, ‘Do we have a controller? Who is the controller? What does the controller do?’” Mohan said. “So my very first thought was, boy, the controller and the state talk about transparency in government. But if people don’t even know we exist, then what kind of transparency do we have here?” Rakesh Mohan Mohan said he views the controller’s job as looking over taxpayer dollars that go to the state. The job also includes overseeing payroll for all state employees and making sure the right amount of money goes to the right place at the right time. Mohan said the office is responsible for statewide accounting and the state’s large data systems. “It may sound boring to most people, but it is an extremely important job,” Mohan said. “And the controller is also responsible for paying all the bills. That includes multi-million dollar contracts.” Mohan has two adult children and three grandchildren. He was married to his wife, Carolyn, for 44 years until she died in 2024. Meet incumbent Republican State Controller Brandon Woolf Woolf first started at the Idaho State Controller’s Office as an intern in 1997 after graduating from Utah State University. He worked his way up to become payroll division administrator and, eventually, chief of staff for former Idaho State Controller Donna Jones. After Jones was seriously injured in a car accident in 2012, former Gov. Butch Otter appointed Woolf to finish Jones’ term while she focused on her recovery. Woolf ran for the position himself and won in 2014. He is finishing his third term of his own as state controller. Woolf said he thinks of the controller’s office as the “checkbook side” of the state government. items.body: Idaho Education News’ board of directors announced today CEO Jennifer Swindell has been named publisher and Devin Bodkin has been named COO and managing editor of the nonprofit, online news organization. Swindell founded Idaho EdNews in January of 2013 and has served as CEO and managing editor over its 14-year development. She will continue to serve as the company’s CEO. Jennifer Swindell, Idaho EdNews founder and publisher “Jennifer is an extraordinary leader and journalist,” said EdNews Board Chair Alicia Ritter. “This promotion is recognition of her success at growing an organization whose consistent and solid news reporting has elevated thoughtful and impactful discussion of education in Idaho.” Bodkin spent the last year as EdNews’ assistant managing editor, prepping for today’s promotion. Previously, he was an East Idaho reporter, blogger and editor for EdNews. He will continue to work and live in eastern Idaho. “We’re lucky to have a talent like Devin take the reins of EdNews management,” Ritter said. “His experience, talent and perspective will serve readers well as he steps into big shoes.” Swindell is an award-winning investigative journalist and editor and has been an Idaho journalist for nearly 40 years. She spent 20 years at the Idaho Statesman as a reporter, columnist and editor. She also was a director of communications for Boise State University before launching EdNews. As publisher, Swindell will set the strategic vision of Idaho EdNews and continue to be the public face of the organization. Bodkin previously was a corporate editor at the Idaho National Laboratory and a former Idaho teacher. As managing editor, he will be responsible for day-to-day operations. EdNews, a non-profit, is governed by a three-person board, including Ritter. Also serving on the board are Kim O’Connor, a former journalist and victim witness coordinator for the Ada County Prosecutor’s Office, and Stacia Albiston, a former teacher and the communications officer for the J.A. and Kathryn Albertson Family Foundation. Devin Bodkin, Idaho EdNews COO and managing editor In other staff news, Ryan Suppe is being promoted to accountability reporter and assistant managing editor. He’ll pursue watchdog stories and assist Bodkin with day-to-day operations. Suppe was EdNews’ politics reporter. Sean Dolan will move into the politics reporter position and cover the Idaho Legislature with veteran reporter Kevin Richert, who has covered the Legislature for more than 35 years with the Idaho Statesman and Idaho Education News. Richert also will continue to write his Thursday analysis pieces and anchor the new Idaho EdNews Show, a regular podcast-video. Emma Epperly will continue to serve as EdNews North Idaho reporter, rounding out a team whose reporting reaches all corners of the state. She also follows charter school development and how policies are implemented in Idaho schools. EdNews has won multiple national and statewide awards for investigative and watchdog journalism. The website has seen record growth this past year, reaching millions of page views and social media followers. EdNews produces comprehensive and thoughtful journalism about education policy and practice in Idaho. The nonprofit is a public awareness service where parents, patrons, educators and lawmakers can find the most useful information on issues that affect Idaho’s children and their future. EdNews is committed to its mission of holding lawmakers and educators accountable for taxpayer dollars and student achievement. EdNews is free and published without advertising thanks to the generosity of the J.A. and Kathryn Albertson Family Foundation. For questions or comments, contact Jennifer at jswindell@idahoednews.org . items.body: The Boise Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as seen on Feb. 5, 2025. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has donated $1 million to an Idaho political action committee, or PAC, opposing the abortion rights initiative on the ballot this November. The donation went to the Too Extreme for Idaho Political Action Committee, which opposes the initiative. “While The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints remains neutral toward political candidates, it actively addresses ballot initiatives it believes carry significant moral consequences,” the church said in a statement. “Accordingly, the Church has joined a coalition of like-minded organizations and individuals in Idaho to dedicate resources toward defeating Proposition 1.” Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions If passed, the voter initiative would repeal Idaho’s abortion laws, enumerate rights related to reproductive health, and create liability protections for healthcare providers who provide abortion and other reproductive healthcare. The Idaho Falls radio station NewsTalk 107.9 first reported the donation on Thursday. The Idaho Capital Sun confirmed the donation with a spokesperson for the church on Friday. The large donation comes after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador published an opinion in August that says churches are allowed to donate money to political campaigns — including for and against Proposition 1 — without disclosing their donors, as long as they don’t ask members to donate specifically for the campaign, Boise State Public Radio reported. Leaders from the church, widely known as the Mormon church, issued a letter against Prop 1 in September, the Salt Lake Tribune reported. The letter was read to congregations last month, the church’s assistant communications director Brian Whitlock said in an email. “Our long-held stance on abortion remains clear and unchanged,” the four-member U.S. Central Area Presidency of the LDS Church wrote in the letter. The church, which opposes elective abortions, posted its stance on abortion online . It allows for possible exemptions in cases of rape and incest, if a “competent physician determines that the life or health of the mother is in serious jeopardy,” or a “competent physician determines that the fetus has severe defects that will not allow the baby to survive beyond birth.” “Even these exceptions do not automatically justify abortion,” the statement said. “Abortion is a most serious matter. It should be considered only after the persons responsible have received confirmation through prayer.” Idaho’s abortion ban allows the procedure to prevent the death of the mother and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors who provide abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties, including minimum prison time, and potential civil lawsuits brought by family members of the aborted fetus. items.body: President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel, but on Friday, Idaho Gov. Brad Little relaxed the Gem State's inspections of the fuel during harvest. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed an executive order Friday to suspend for 30 days state inspections of dyed diesel fuel in an attempt to lower costs for farmers and ranchers, according to the governor’s office. With election pressure mounting, states move to suspend fuel taxes Dyed diesel is diesel fuel with red dye in it and is exempt from federal and state motor fuel taxes. The tax-exempt fuel is only meant for certain approved off-road uses, such as for farming equipment, construction equipment and home heating. The dye helps regulators enforce this requirement. Idaho’s average diesel price was around $6.41 per gallon as of Friday, according to AAA fuel prices. Prices for oil products have risen this year largely because of restrictions on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz amid the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran, which have disrupted global supply chains. Diesel supplies have been in particularly short supply, NPR reported, and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have also affected global supplies. On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel. President Donald Trump hands off a newly signed executive order waiving federal taxes on red-dyed diesel to aide Natalie Harp during a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner) Little’s order signed Friday directs Idaho State Police and the Idaho Transportation Department to suspend inspection for dyed diesel while the agencies review Idaho’s policies and procedures, his office announced in a press release. The review will consider other state’s approach to dyed diesel enforcement and the agencies will make recommendations to Little for “efficient, effective, and practical inspection,” the release said. Little said in the press release that the timing of the order is meant to ease costs during harvest season. “Idaho farmers and ranchers work hard to feed our families, our country, and the world,” Little said in the release. “President Trump has made cutting red tape a priority, and Idaho is doing the same. We will continue looking for ways to give our farmers, ranchers, and working men and women on the road more freedom to do what they do best.” Legislative leaders in written statements said they supported the governor’s decision. “Idaho farmers and ranchers are facing high costs across the board, and expensive diesel is adding to the pressure during harvest,” Senate President Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon, R-Declo, said in the release. “This order provides some immediate relief while giving the state time to review these requirements and find a practical approach that supports our producers without adding unnecessary costs or red tape.” House Speaker Mike Moyle , R-Star, said suspending the inspections while the state reviews its policies “is a practical approach that puts common sense first and gives Idaho producers one less thing to worry about during harvest.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. Through the first three months of Fiscal Year 2027, state revenues are now up by $90.3 million, or 6.8%. The surging revenues in this year’s state budget are a stark contrast to last year, when Little and Idaho state legislators approved near across-the-board budget cuts for almost all state agencies, programs and departments to pay for federal tax cuts President Donald Trump signed into law through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to ensure the state passed a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. State revenues were also up in July and August. “Idaho’s strong revenue growth is encouraging and reflects the strength of our economy, but we must remain disciplined and make spending decisions based on what we can responsibly sustain,” Little said in a written statement Friday afternoon. “The difficult decisions we made last year put us in a stronger fiscal position, and we need to continue prioritizing the investments that matter most to Idahoans while protecting our long-term financial stability.” Income tax withholdings are driver of state revenue increase Individual income tax withholdings are a big part of the revenue increase. The September General Fund Revenue Report said individual income tax collections are up 18.3% fiscal year to date. “It appears that employees are getting lots of hours of work and that there may be some bonus activity being paid by employers,” Idaho Division of Financial Management officials wrote in the September revenue report. items.body: The mental health of our children is on everyone’s mind, including school leaders. That’s why 10 rural districts and charter schools jumped at the chance to apply for mental health support through Idaho’s Rural Health Transformation Program. The plans included counseling, telehealth, and behavioral health coordinators to help students and families connect with care. Their work was wasted when a Republican-only interim committee voted to shut down the opportunity and redirect $1.2 million. The documented need was high. In Notus, 46% of surveyed junior high and high school students identified mental health as a concern, and the district sought $60,000 for a coordinator serving students from preschool through 12th grade. Aberdeen wanted to expand counseling and wellness services in a community where some care is 20 to 50 minutes away. The decision is hard to understand, but it fits a pattern from the Republican supermajority: cutting investments in mental health. Last year, Idaho eliminated Assertive Community Treatment, or ACT, along with peer support services, as years of tax cuts for the wealthy left less money for essential services. ACT provided intensive, mobile care for people with severe mental illness. Providers and law enforcement warned that people would end up in crisis without those supports. Soon, visits to eastern Idaho crisis centers had increased by 34% in December and 43% in January compared with the year before. Providers reported rising hospitalizations and more pressure on jails. Four former ACT patients died after the program was cut, compared with one reported death during the previous 18 months. After months of warnings and advocacy from mental health practitioners, lawmakers pieced together one-time funding to bring ACT and peer support back. That meant providers had to fight to restore services instead of focusing on patients in their communities. But the future of those services remains uncertain. These cuts were not just cruel. They were shortsighted from a budget perspective, too. Providers estimated ACT cost less than $100 per patient per day, while untreated illness can lead to repeated hospitalizations, court hearings, and jail stays that cost taxpayers far more. When elected officials disregard the health and safety of our communities, there should be accountability. The Rural Health Transformation Committee is made up of eight Republican lawmakers, including Reps. Dori Healey and Dustin Manwaring. Both are now up for reelection in two of the most competitive legislative districts in Idaho. Voters in those districts should take a hard look at this record. Blocking mental health resources for rural families after Idaho has already seen the consequences of cutting care is the kind of decision that should carry real political consequences. The Republicans who made this decision had the chance to learn from what happened. Now voters do too.

items.body: The Idaho Public Charter School Commission approved applications for two new schools Thursday — with some conditions. Doral Academy of Idaho, a K-8 charter school in Meridian, plans to add grades 9-12 at a second campus. Elevate Academy, a network of career-technical charters, is also preparing a new CTE-focused school serving grades 6-12 in Pocatello. Before they open, however, school leaders must prove to the charter commission that they have balanced operating budgets along with lease or purchase agreements for their buildings. They must also hand over copies of all grants, loans and contracts they’ve secured to fund and operate the schools. The charter commission unanimously voted to approve the schools with conditions. If the conditions aren’t satisfied, school openings could be delayed or the commission’s approval of their applications could be revoked. Doral Academy Preparatory Doral Academy will add a second campus, also in Meridian, that serves middle and high schoolers. The new school, Doral Academy Preparatory, will be 6-12 while the current school moves to K-5. Doral Academy is an “arts-integration” school, which means it uses arts as a method of instruction in all subjects, said Sara Frost, chairwoman of the charter’s board of directors. “We want to continue growing that into a high school experience that will continue to be a very vibrant and enriching education for our students.” Doral Academy leaders plan to launch the preparatory school next year, welcoming ninth-graders in the fall. Additional grades will be added in subsequent years after the new building in south Meridian is ready. The new school will have sports and house 840 students at full capacity, Frost told the commission. School leaders are banking on Meridian’s continued growth to fill the halls. Their presentation pointed to thousands of new residential units coming to south Meridian. items.body: Boise State University’s 10-year campus master plan has buy-in at City Hall. The Boise City Council signed off Tuesday on the university’s land use plan, the Idaho Statesman reported . This vote links the university’s plan and the city’s comprehensive land use plan. The 10-year university plan is designed to accommodate projected growth at Idaho’s largest four-year university — by adding 750 dormitory beds, 370 parking spaces and 270 staff members. The top priority is a $140 million science research building, a 90,000- to 110,000-square-foot project that would go up on the southern fringe of campus. Designed to address the university’s shortage of research space, the new building is scheduled to come online in 2029. The dorm space will focus on two areas of need: housing for first-year students and graduate student housing. City Hall will still get a say on specific projects. “While we’re approving a master plan, we’re not approving any specific plans,” said council member Jimmy Hallyburton, according to a Statesman report on the Tuesday meeting. “Those things would have to come back before council.” More reading: Click here for an in-depth April article on Boise State’s 10-year plan.

items.body: A federal school choice super PAC announced Thursday that it has endorsed Gov. Brad Little for reelection. The AFC Victory Fund, a political action committee affiliated with the American Federation for Children, stated in a press release that Little has supported “significant school choice expansion,” citing the $50 million Parental Choice Tax Credit, the Idaho Launch grant program and opting in to the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit. Tommy Schultz, CEO of the AFC Victory Fund, said Little has empowered families to “choose the education that best fits their child’s needs, abilities and aspirations.” “Idahoans are demanding school choice, and elected leaders are responding,” Schultz said in the press release. “We are proud to endorse Governor Brad Little for reelection and look forward to working alongside him and other Idaho leaders committed to delivering school choice for every family.” Gov. Brad Little speaks at the Idaho School Administrators Association 2026 Summer Leadership Conference at the Grove Hotel in Boise on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Brad Little speaks at the Idaho School Administrators Association 2026 Summer Leadership Conference at the Grove Hotel in Boise on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. (Sean Dolan/EdNews) Little in 2025 signed House Bill 93 , creating the Parental Choice Tax Credit, allowing parents with kids in nonpublic schools to apply for $5,000 per child, or $7,500 for children with disabilities, to cover private school tuition or homeschool expenses. In 2023, Little signed House Bill 24 , creating the Idaho Launch grant program for graduating high school seniors. Students can apply for up to $8,000 in tuition support for in-demand career programs. “Together, LAUNCH and the PCTC made Idaho the first state to offer education freedom from kindergarten through career,” the press release stated. This year, Little signed an executive order opting Idaho into a federal school choice tax credit under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The AFC Victory Fund’s press release this week used similar language in Little’s February statement. “Idaho is proud to be the only state offering education freedom from kindergarten through career,” Little said in a February press release. “My executive order strengthens our commitment to ensuring every parent has the opportunity to choose the education environment that best fits their child.” The American Federation for Children in April terminated the Idaho Federation for Children PAC, which spent $432,923 in 2024 to elect school choice candidates, and is now using the federal super PAC AFC Victory Fund to make independent expenditures in Idaho’s elections. The super PAC spent $105,517 on the May primaries. While the school choice group is supporting Little, the statewide Idaho Education Association teachers’ union in April issued a vote of no-confidence in the governor.

items.body: For 80 minutes Tuesday night, Terri Pickens and John Stegner agreed about almost everything. Especially Brad Little. Sharing a stage at a Boise junior high school auditorium, Pickens and Stegner took turns laying out a litany of criticisms. Little is too deferential to President Donald Trump. Little compromises too much with House Speaker Mike Moyle and other conservative lawmakers. Little is wrong on private school choice. Wrong about opening Idaho to, potentially, thousands of tons of nuclear waste shipments . Weak on public lands. Too often silent. Pickens, an attorney, and Stegner, a retired judge, presented a case for the prosecution. An audience of about 150 people murmured their approval, applauded on occasion, and snickered at the zingers. Little provided no defense. The two-term governor was a no-show for the League of Women Voters forum . A folding chair, reserved for Little, sat vacant. A bottle of water remained unopened. Gubernatorial candidates Terri Pickens and John Stegner field questions at an Oct. 6, 2026 League of Women Voters forum at South Junior High School in Boise. Incumbent Gov. Brad Little was invited, but did not attend. (Kevin Richert/Idaho EdNews) With 10 minutes left in the forum, Stegner openly addressed the elephant not in the room. “He’s away without official leave, including the fact that he isn’t here tonight.” It’s a governor’s race with three major candidates and two decidedly different approaches. Pickens, a Democrat, and Stegner, an independent, are crisscrossing the state. In stump speeches and joint appearances, they are desperately trying to take the fight to the incumbent. Meanwhile, the Republican Little seems content to avoid public appearances in general and debates in particular , banking on a big fundraising advantage and the name ID that comes with 25 years in public office. Nonetheless, the three candidates will appear together once. At least by name, on the Nov. 3 ballot. Little: A long and complicated education resume There is an adage in politics, seemingly not in practice in this race. When incumbents are worried about staff or volunteer complacency, they say they want to campaign as if they are 20 points behind in the polls. If any such worry exists in the Little camp, it’s under wraps — much like Little himself. Little’s campaign declined an EdNews interview request and asked for written questions. Campaign manager Joan Vargas did not answer EdNews’ question about Little’s decision to skip debates and joint appearances. “Gov. items.body: Voters cast their ballots during the May 19, 2026, primary election at The Waterfront in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) This year, Idaho voters have a lot to decide on: Who will be the state’s next governor or U.S. senator? Should two constitutional amendments pass? Should voters pass their own law to repeal the state’s abortion ban? 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More But in the mix is a poll that the Idaho Legislature called for: What should be the state’s official gun? Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. The state Legislature considered a bill this year to allow members of the public to carry concealed guns inside parts of courthouses that aren’t meant for court, like offices for county commissioners and clerks. The advisory question on the ballot this year asks voters to weigh in on the Legislature’s possible decision to declare a firearm — out of a mix of well-known Western and American guns — as Idaho’s official state gun. If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols , like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. Ten other states have declared state guns , according to the National Rifle Association, a prominent gun lobbying group. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho lawmaker hopes the advisory question will boost voter turnout One of the lawmakers behind the push for the ballot question, Rep. Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said he thought it might drum up voter turnout during a year when many consequential issues are on the ballot. In election years when the president isn’t on the ballot, like this year, fewer voters tend to participate. “Voter turnout is always important,” he said in an interview. “… When you have a lot of voter apathy, I think we don’t get as good of results as we could if we had an informed electorate that was actually out and voting.” The votes won’t be the final say. “The results,” the bill says, “will guide the Legislature as to which gun shall be designated the state gun of Idaho.” Idaho Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, and Idaho House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, walk Gov. Brad Little out of the House chambers after the governor delivered his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) But Monks said this is the only time he knows of when the state sought public input before designating a state item. Monks acknowledges that not everyone loves the idea of declaring a state gun. “I don’t think you can make everybody always happy. The majority of people in Idaho do have guns,” he said. “We have a pretty high percentage of gun ownership in our state. And so I think it reflects the fact that Idaho is a very gun-friendly state, and that it is an important part of our culture in many aspects.” He stressed that the push for the ballot question didn’t take much time. “I had some people ask me, ‘How come this is your priority?’ I’m like, ‘Well, this isn’t my priority. It’s just something we did kind of on the side,’” Monks said. “I put in 12 to 14 hour days there all the time, and I can tell you I spent very little time on this particular issue. items.body: U.S. Attorney for the District of Idaho Bart Davis in his Boise office. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho . ‘The best job I ever had’: Bart Davis returns as Idaho’s chief federal litigator Davis, who is 71 and in his second term as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, will retire Oct. 17, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho said. “I am unable to overstate the privilege it has been to work with the dedicated and remarkable women and men of the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Davis said in a written statement. “These great lawyers and support staff faithfully enforce the law, work to keep Idaho and our country safe, support our law enforcement partners and protect the civil rights of others. I am proud of the work they do every day.” President Donald Trump nominated Davis for U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho last year, and the U.S. Senate confirmed Davis on Oct. 7, 2025 – exactly one year before Davis announced his retirement. Davis previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho from 2017 to 2021 during Trump’s first term. Prior to serving as U.S. attorney, Davis practiced law in Idaho Falls and served in the Idaho Senate for 19 years. Davis, a Republican, served as Senate majority leader for 15 years, where he was regarded as a powerful and intelligent legislative leader. “Bart Davis has served the State of Idaho and our country with distinction throughout a remarkable career,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a written statement. “His sound legal judgment, deep knowledge of Idaho and unwavering commitment to doing what is right have been invaluable to our state.” Davis also served as co-chairman of the 2021 Idaho Commission for Reapportionment , which was charged with redrawing Idaho’s congressional and legislative boundaries following the 2020 census to ensure political representation is proportional. During a 2025 interview with the Idaho Capital Sun, Davis called serving as U.S. attorney, “the best job I ever had.” “… to work with these people who are genuinely trying to even-handedly apply the laws of the United States of America,” Davis said. “It impressed me then, and it impresses me now.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Governor says Davis strengthened relationship between Justice Department and Idaho Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho is responsible for prosecuting federal crimes in Idaho, defends the United States in civil cases and collects debts owed to the United States, the office said. In the past year under Davis’ leadership, the office said it has filed 298 criminal charges, including 103 drug trafficking cases, 89 violent crimes cases, 69 immigration cases and 22 fraud cases. “During his time as U.S. Attorney for Idaho, Bart strengthened the relationship between Idaho and the U.S. Department of Justice and represented our state with integrity and professionalism,” Little said. “ We will miss his counsel, his wisdom and his steady leadership. I am grateful for Bart’s many years of service and friendship, and I wish him all the best as he enters retirement and has more time to enjoy with his wife, children and grandchildren.” Davis and his wife, Marion, have six children and 14 grandchildren. Davis and Marion recently celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.body: Independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles, left, and Independent Leadership Council co-founder Adam Brandon speak about Achilles' commitment to not caucus with either major party, to only serve two terms, hold public town halls and participate in debates if elected. Achilles held the press conference on Oct. 7, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles on Wednesday pledged to not caucus with either party if he’s elected. 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More Achilles, who served in the Idaho Legislature as a Democrat before announcing his independent run for U.S. Senate, is running against incumbent Republican Sen. Jim Risch , who’s in his 18th year as a senator. Achilles was joined at the Idaho state Capitol in Boise by Adam Brandon, the co-founder of a national advocacy organization promoting independent candidates called the Independent Leadership Council . Achilles also committed to serve a maximum of two terms, hold town halls in each of Idaho’s 44 counties every two years, and to engage in public debates. Brandon previously was president of FreedomWorks, which helped tea party candidates get elected to office. That organization dissolved in 2024 , Politico reported. “Every vote that he casts, both parties are going to have to come to him for his vote to represent the state of Idaho, and I think that is incredibly, incredibly powerful,” Brandon said. Idaho US Senate candidates weigh in on tariffs, Iran War, federal spending and more In the letter Achilles signed to make these commitments, he said the U.S. Senate rules would still guarantee him a committee seat despite not caucusing with the major parties. The two independent U.S. senators — Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont — both caucus with Senate Democrats. When King won his election in 2012, he announced he would caucus with the Democrats because it would allow him to participate more in the committee process, PBS News reported at the time. Committee assignments are largely decided by party leaders and then formally voted on by the entire Senate. During the event, Achilles also signed a sworn, notarized statement that would resign him from office in 2039 — meaning if elected, he would only be able to serve two, six-year terms. A spokesman for the Achilles campaign said the letter will be sent to either the governor’s office or secretary of state to keep. “We’re serious about this,” Achilles said Wednesday. “That’s it. I don’t want to spend more than 12 years in D.C. I love Idaho’s mountains. I want to get back here and get my skis on and do what I love doing. So two terms. That’s it.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. According to an online petition , members of Timberline’s football team used Snapchat to “call for a female student to be raped and killed.” Police began investigating the reported threats last week after Timberline officials contacted Boise police. District officials have said police asked the district to pause its own investigation to avoid interference with the case.
