items.body: Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest proposed cuts to the state's Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun) One thing we know for absolute certain in Idaho: Our people understand the value of Medicaid expansion. We voted to adopt Medicaid expansion in 2018 through ballot initiative started after years of inaction by the state Legislature, with more than 60 percent of Idaho voters supporting expanded healthcare access. When the state Legislature became very active in attempts to weaken and repeal that voter-approved expansion seemingly as soon as they could, Idahoans showed up. They traveled to Boise to let lawmakers know that the program was not a suggestion, but a mandate and more than 80,000 of our friends, family and neighbors relied on it. Idaho’s Medicaid work requirements start in January. Here’s how they will work. Some of the busiest days at the Capitol are when everyday Idahoans show up to have their voices heard on a healthcare bill when lawmakers have tried to repeal the program or institute confusing bureaucracy via work requirements. The halls are packed and hearing rooms overflow with Medicaid supporters who vastly outnumber those who advocate cuts at around 100-1 … and the one is very often not somebody from Idaho. Most Idahoans, myself included, don’t think much about the details of our health insurance until we need it. For someone with cancer, that could mean discovering at a doctor’s appointment, while scheduling a scan, or even in the middle of treatment or recovery that they no longer have Medicaid coverage due to the work requirements that will add red tape to the program starting in January. Then what? Do they delay treatment while trying to navigate the paperwork? Do they skip a follow-up appointment or prescription they can no longer afford? For most, there isn’t another insurance option waiting in the wings. These are Idahoans who already qualified for Medicaid, including people whose serious medical conditions should qualify them for a medical frailty exemption. Administrative red tape should not become another obstacle between a cancer patient and the care they need. When that happens, the consequences aren’t limited to the patient. Their families suffer too and local care providers must then care for somebody with no ability to pay the bill. It’s a terrible scenario and one Medicaid expansion has prevented from being widescale. This past session, House Bill 913 established the Jan. 1 start date for federally mandated work requirements. Medicaid proponents had requested a one-year extension to give the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and our residents more time to learn about the changes and implementation. That did not happen, so we hope Idaho lawmakers grasp fully their responsibility to hold true to the promises they made clearly and often during all those Boise debates over work requirements. Then, they were firm in their convictions that no eligible person would ever be stripped of healthcare. Policymakers should be just as committed now to making work requirement exemptions clear and accessible as they were about putting them into law. Coverage losses from work requirements usually aren’t because someone suddenly became ineligible, but because eligible people get caught in paperwork, reporting requirements, missed notices or other government bureaucracy. Boise school officials have called off homecoming activities at Timberline High School, as police investigate an online threat targeting a Timberline student. Originally, district officials had planned to postpone the homecoming football game, which had been scheduled for Thursday. But on Tuesday evening, the district canceled the game, which Timberline will now forfeit. “Given the seriousness of the circumstances involving recent student social media posts and ongoing concerns about student safety and well-being, we believe cancellation is the most responsible decision,” Superintendent Wendy Johnson, district Area Director Shelley Bonds and Timberline Principal Chad Wright said in an email to district families and staff. “Our priority is ensuring students and staff are safe and supported while providing the Timberline school community time to process what has occurred.” On Tuesday afternoon, in a separate email to Timberline families and staff, district and school leaders said “growing concerns over student safety” factored into their postponement decision. “This is not a decision made easily or lightly,” Johnson, Bonds and Wright wrote. “Homecoming is so much more than one game, one parade or one dance, it is a celebration of current, future and past students and the families, educators and community who support them. However, given the heightened emotions, threats of violence, and the simple need to pause, reflect and process, we believe it is not only the prudent decision, but the right one as well.” An “additional police presence” is on site at Timberline, district officials said in a question-and-answer page on the reported threat. Boise school officials have called the reported threat “disturbing.” However, the district and the Boise Police Department have said little about the case — which began to unfold Friday, when school officials contacted Boise Police’s school resource officer unit. “With an active investigation and the potential involvement of minors, we are limited to what we can share,” Johnson, Bonds and Wright said in a Sunday evening message to Timberline parents and staff. “While respecting privacy limits, we want to be as open, honest and transparent as possible to assure you that there is zero tolerance for the type of behavior and language attributed to any member of our school community. items.body: Last summer, Mackay High history teacher Jess Johnson listened to an audiobook about the USS Indianapolis on a trip home from Mount Rushmore. The story sparked Johnson’s interest in Lt. Cmdr. Earl Henry Sr., the ship’s dentist and an avid bird painter and taxidermist. Henry died after a Japanese submarine torpedoed the ship in July 1945. The ship sank in about 12 minutes, killing hundreds of crewmen. Johnson learned that Henry’s son, Earl Henry Jr., sold prints of his father’s work. One painting, “American Eagle in the Pacific,” was completed on the ship before it sank. It depicts an eagle holding a tattered Japanese flag. Johnson ordered a copy. “A nd maybe 20 minutes after I purchased it, he calls me,” Johnson said. The phone call kicked off a lifelong friendship between Johnson and Henry Jr. — and became the foundation for a unit in Johnson’s military history class at Mackay High. It’s just one of dozens of out-of-the-box approaches Johnson uses to bring history to life for his students. “It’s our lives — it’s what happens,” he said. “I try to make the connection between the old and the new.” Click to view slideshow. A teacher in the making Johnson grew up on a farm outside of Preston. He wasn’t “that good of a student” but sports had an impact. By eighth grade, his coaches influenced him to become a teacher. After high school, he started a family and worked nights as a cheesemaker. He fit classes into a busy schedule. With six kids, it took Johnson seven years to finish his teaching degree. He graduated from Utah State University in 1990 and took his first teaching job in Yuma, Arizona, the next fall. He taught middle school classes and coached at the high school. Coaching came easy — teaching did not. “I was drowning, and my principal said, ‘You’re not a very good teacher and you’re not going to make it,'” Johnson recalls. He eventually partnered with a veteran teacher, who encouraged him to be himself, stay calm, and push through ups and downs. That changed everything, Johnson said. He soon fell in love with the job — and with history. ‘I said heck yeah’ Johnson eventually made his way back to Idaho. After nearly two decades teaching at American Falls High, he and some other coaches earned their master’s degrees. He took a job as principal of Mackay High Jr./Sr. School, where his children graduated. Johnson moved around after becoming an empty nester. Three years ago, his sons moved back to Mackay and asked him to move closer. “I said heck yeah,” Johnson said. He returned to Mackay to teach history, government, and coach junior high school football — and continue his emphasis on projects. ‘I don’t go into the book’ “My style is probably different than a traditional history teacher,” Johnson said. “I don’t go into the book. Students dress up as Roman soldiers with homemade armor, make hardtack, make their own gas masks to test with a fog machine, dress up as 1920s flappers and set up a faux speakeasy. At 65, the projects keep Johnson excited about teaching. “It really makes it meaningful,” he said. For him, history is key to helping students understand the world around them. items.body: A voter casts his ballot in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More Currently, there are two ways in Idaho that marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs can be legalized and regulated. First, the Idaho Legislature could pass a law to legalize it. Second, Idaho voters could legalize it by passing a ballot initiative. Who gets to decide is a big part of the debate over House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR 4 for short. House Joint Resolution 4 is a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would give the Idaho Legislature the sole authority and power to legalize marijuana (including medical marijuana), narcotics and other psychoactive substances. If a simple majority of voters vote “yes” for House Joint Resolution 4, Idahoans would not be allowed to bring a ballot initiative forward to legalize marijuana, medical cannabis, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. If voters vote “no” and don’t approve HJR 4, there would be no changes to the Idaho Constitution. That means Idahoans would still be able to use the ballot initiative process to legalize marijuana, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. Voters in several of Idaho’s neighboring states, including Washington, Oregon, Montana and Nevada, used ballot initiatives to legalize marijuana in those states. People have tried to do the same in Idaho. But so far, each effort has failed to meet the signature-gathering requirements to qualify for an election, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. items.body: Joleen Noble, executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank, says the nonprofit organization typically provides more than 75,000 diapers to children in need per month. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Diaper Bank) As a mother of two small children (ages 2 and 5), there’s no need to lecture Jolleen Noble of Meridian about the cost of diapers – which could run close to $200 a month per child. And there’s no need to talk to her about other paycheck-eating costs such as daycare, medical emergencies and clothing. She knows all about the challenges of making ends meet. Noble, of course, can’t solve all of the financial problems. But as the executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank , she’s providing some welcome relief in at least one area. And there are no forms to fill out, or financial statements to submit. “People who need diapers need our help,” she said. There are limits. Noble’s nonprofit organization will provide up to 50 diapers a month per baby, which doesn’t cover the entire cost for diapers. But it does make the monthly diaper tab less daunting. “Diapers are expensive, and they just add to the cost of everything else,” she said. The diaper bank gets a large portion of its supply from the National Diaper Bank Network, buying bulk from manufacturers and regional diaper drives. Mary Kay Link, an Idaho Diaper Bank board member for seven years, sees how the organization helps mothers and families. She volunteers with the Holy Apostles St. Vincent de Paul of Meridian , one of 43 working partners that distribute diapers. “SVDP has many single moms who work and need food and diapers to make ends meet. Saving money on diapers allows them to use the money to pay bills or put gas in their car,” she said. Noble has been the executive director for almost a year, and demands for the service are growing. “When the diaper bank started in 2014, they were giving out 8,000 diapers a month, and when I started it was 50,000 per month. Typically, we give out 75,000 to 100,000 per month … last month we gave 119,000.” Noble says that level of growth would not happen without her board of directors. “We have an incredible all-volunteer board that has helped shape Idaho Diaper Bank into what it is today,” she said. “I would not be in the position I am today, or able to do what I do, without the support, leadership and willingness to jump in wherever they are needed.” The diaper bank’s 43 partners also contribute to the success. Susan Rohrbacher sees the needed help through Parma Community Schools, which serves more than 25 babies per month. “This partnership has been especially meaningful for families of children with special needs,” she said. “The Idaho Diaper Bank is truly making a difference by easing financial stress and helping our families feel supported and cared for.” As with other nonprofit organizations, Noble sees challenges. “The biggest need is sustainable funding that allows us to grow our reach. Our funding comes from grants and in-kind donations. There is no government assistance,” she said. “Simply put, if we want to send more diapers out the door, we have to bring more diapers and funding in the door,” Noble said. “Space is becoming another challenge. As we think about serving more families and potentially expanding, sustainable funding and the capacity to store the product becomes increasingly important.” One big way individuals and businesses can help is through diaper drives. “Some of my favorite moments are seeing people in the community rally around a diaper drive,” she said. “Those drives bring in product and monetary donations, of course, but they also get people talking about diaper needs and introduce people to our mission. It’s pretty incredible to watch.” The Idaho Diaper Bank is living up to its slogan, “Changing Babies. Changing Lives.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: Trained staff members could carry guns in the Marsing and Homedale school districts if local leaders move forward with safety programs modeled after one in the Kimberly district . As first reported by the Owyhee County Avalanche, Marsing Superintendent Norm Stewart and Homedale Superintendent Rob Sauer will present policies to their respective school boards this month that would lay out trainings for staffers selected to carry concealed firearms. Sauer will propose a policy for armed staff at a Monday, Oct. 12, board meeting. Stewart will propose a similar policy to Marsing trustees at a Tuesday, Oct. 13, meeting. Marsing’s plan would reflect Kimberly’s policy “ as much as possible,” Stewart said. That could mean adopting it entirely. Sauer said Homedale intends to do the same. The Kimberly district, located near Twin Falls, rolled out its program last year and modeled it after one at Xavier Charter School. In August, a gunman killed three people at an In-N-Out drive-thru in Twin Falls. At least three school shootings have occurred in Idaho throughout the last four decades, but none have resulted in a death. Most recently, in 2021 , a Rigby sixth grader shot two students and a custodian. All three victims survived non-life-threatening injuries. “ This is not something we’re excited about,” Sauer said. “ We just recognize the times we live in, and that we need to do our best to deter and delay so law enforcement can do their job and protect our students.” The policies would allow some staffers to carry concealed firearms on campus, Stewart and Sauer said. Staff members would first need an enhanced concealed carry permit from the county. County sheriffs issue the permits. In Owyhee County, where Marsing and Homedale are located, residents fill out a form to receive a permit. Staff members would then have to volunteer to carry a concealed weapon and receive approval from the school board. They would undergo a physical fitness exam, and the districts would hire a third party to perform psychological evaluations. Once volunteers pass their tests, they would begin 40 hours of training. Marsing and Homedale have not identified who would train the volunteers, but they anticipate working with the Owyhee County Sheriff’s Office. Volunteers would then have to complete at least 16 hours of additional training each year. The districts would pay for training and ammunition but would not buy guns or pay volunteers for their training hours. Volunteers would not receive extra pay. “This is strictly voluntary, and you’re doing it because you want to do it for the right reasons: protecting students and staff,” said Stewart. Neither superintendent had estimates for what the programs would cost. The programs are meant to supplement law enforcement, not replace it, district leaders explained. Armed staff members can buy time against an active shooter when police responses are slower in rural areas. Homedale has a police department of seven full-time officers, according to the agency’s website. Marsing has no police department, and the district’s school resource officer is an Owyhee County sheriff’s deputy, one of around 16 officers at the agency, according to 2024 budget reporting on Transparent Idaho . Gun ownership is prevalent in Idaho, where concealed carry is legal without a permit. A 2020 RAND Corporation study estimated around 0.6 guns per Idaho household. Guns are also a part of the state’s culture: In November, Idahoans will vote for the official state gun. School boards in some districts have allowed staff members to carry guns for more than a decade. In January, the West Ada district introduced armed security guards called “campus sentinels.” As state funding for schools stagnates and districts struggle to balance their budgets, school safety can take a hit. items.body: The rotunda of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) When two mental health clinic owners in Idaho set out to restore critical services for people with severe mental illness, they faced an uphill battle. The Idaho Legislature was gearing up for across-the-board budget cuts. But Laura Scuri and Ric Boyce armed lawmakers with information and data — and spent time talking to journalists when four patients died after the mobile treatment service had been cut. Ric Boyce, director of Mental Health Specialists, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel on Dec. 15, 2025 in Rexburg. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The two often worked behind the scenes, directly with lawmakers instead of testifying before committees. “We formed individual relationships with half the Legislature pretty much,” Boyce recalled in an interview. In the end, the programs that they advocated served as a rare instance of a budget cut that state lawmakers reversed. On the final day of this year’s legislative session, Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed into law a bill that temporarily restored funding for the programs that the two providers pushed for: the Assertive Community Treatment program, a mobile program for people with severe mental illness, and peer support services, which helps people navigate treatment. After four patients died, Idaho governor approves restoring cut Medicaid mental health programs Now, a mental health nonprofit plans to honor the two. This week, the National Alliance on Mental Illness of Idaho plans to award them both the Kathie Garrett Impact Award, named after a former Idaho lawmaker. In a news release, the nonprofit said the duo’s advocacy “led to the return of those programs.” The award came as a surprise. “I don’t think either one of us were thinking for a second it’s something that would be noticed,” said Boyce, a clinical social worker who owns Mental Health Specialists, a clinic in eastern Idaho’s Chubbuck. “What was important to us was that we were able to get the clients we were working with back into the program they needed so badly. And that was enough.” Scuri, who co-owns Access Behavioral Health Services in Boise, said it’s her first award. “So it’s extra special to me — especially with the environment that we’re in, and all the changes,” she said. items.body: A nine-member committee will begin the search for a new University of Idaho president . The State Board of Education announced the committee Friday, marking the first significant public step in the search. Current U of I President C. Scott Green announced his retirement on Sept. 9 ; he will stay on as president at his alma mater until June 30. Two State Board members will head the search: Shawn Keough of Sandpoint will chair the committee, and Pete Koehler of Caldwell will serve as vice chair. Koehler is a U of I alum. Here’s a look at the rest of the committee members: Chandra Zenner Ford, the U of I’s senior associate to the president, and executive officer of the university’s Boise and Southwest Idaho center. Mya Pronschinske Groza, a U of I marketing professor, and associate dean of the College of Business and Economics. Bill Gilbert, a former State Board member and a 1997 U of I graduate. Phil Reberger, who served as chief of staff to former Idaho Gov. and Sen. Dirk Kempthorne and former Idaho Sen. Steve Symms. Reberger is a 1964 U of I graduate. Clint Marshall, chair of the University of Idaho Foundation. Mary Hasenoehrl, owner of GKH Farms and partner in Gross Farms, Wilder. Dave Whitehead, president of Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories, Pullman, Wash. “We are grateful to these Vandals and community leaders for agreeing to serve,” State Board President Kurt Liebich said in a news release. “President Green has put the university in a strong position, and we are committed to a thorough search that finds a leader who can build on that momentum.” The timetable for the search is not set. However, the U of I has said the State Board hopes to fill the post by spring, before Green’s retirement. Under a new state law , passed this year, the presidential search process is now almost entirely a closed-door process. After private meetings and interviews, the search committee will submit a sole finalist’s name to the State Board. If board members agree to the recommendation, the board can publicly name the finalist and make the hire within 10 business days. The law also sets the guidelines for the makeup of a search committee, composed of at least eight members. With nine members, the U of I committee is slightly larger than the minimum required by law.

(Photo by Chief Mass Communication Specialist Darren M. Moore/U.S. Navy) The campaign for incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch strongly denied these rumors. The more-than-a-century-old law states that if a U.S. senator from Idaho resigns or dies within 30 days of the general election, then the governor could appoint a replacement and “no election for United States senator to fill said vacancy shall be held at such general election.” Risch is running against Todd Achilles, who has taken heat from from Risch’s campaign for running as an independent after serving in the Idaho Legislature as a Democrat. “This rumor is completely false,” Risch’s campaign manager Marc Kilmer told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email. “Jim Risch is leading in the polls. He is running an aggressive campaign. He will be victorious on November 3. This conspiracy theory is being perpetrated by our desperate opponent to take attention away from his liberal record. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Two days after a grand jury indicted a former Idaho state government employee on two felony counts of misuse of public funds, a local judge dismissed the case — after a request from the prosecutor. The case marked the first criminal charges — and a rare public update — to emerge from a yearslong investigation launched by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador that probed how the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare doled out $72 million in federal child care grants in 2021 and 2022. The official who was criminally charged, Ericka Rupp, oversaw the grant program. In the indictment, filed in Canyon County District Court last week, the grand jury charged Rupp with two felony counts of misuse of public funds and securities, for allegedly illegally authorizing, appropriating or otherwise misusing more than $300 of the government’s money. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at the Idaho Medal of Honor ceremony held Sept. 1, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) Labrador’s special prosecutor, Canyon County Prosecuting Attorney Christopher Boyd, told the Idaho Capital Sun that the amount of money allegedly misused was not specified in the indictment, but that it would’ve been an issue to determine during a potential trial. Boyd said he moved to drop the indictment based on feedback from jurors. “I, however, asked of them whether they felt the case was one worth pursuing in terms of resources,” Boyd wrote in a text message. “I truly wanted their opinion on this. They had spent several full days taking testimony. The majority of jurors felt my time was better spent focusing on the many other serious crimes they worked on.” For each count, the penalties could have been up to 14 years imprisonment and up to $10,000 in fines, according to state laws cited in the indictment. Rupp’s attorney, Scott McKay, declined to comment. In a Friday order, Third District Judge Thomas W. Whitney wrote he was dismissing the case upon the state’s request. The court hasn’t released records supporting the judge’s decision to dismiss the case. Special prosecutor Christopher Boyd argues in district court that the Idaho Office of the Attorney General should not pay legal fees associated with litigation that set to block the office’s civil subpoena. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Pending permission from the court, Boyd said he hopes to release a report with more details in the coming days. Asked whether he’d pursue charges against Rupp, or other people linked to the investigation, Boyd said: “The report should conclude my investigation.” The Idaho attorney general’s office could not immediately be reached for comment. Department of Health and Welfare spokesperson Greg Stahl directed questions about the case to parties involved. “(The Department of Health and Welfare) takes seriously its responsibility to be a good steward of taxpayer dollars and remains committed to transparency, accountability, and the appropriate use of public funds,” Stahl said in a statement. items.body: Few things are bipartisan anymore, but on Monday, the U.S. Senate overwhelmingly agreed on a college athletics makeover. Jeramiah Dickey More money for student-athletes. Less money for agents. Fewer player transfers. Limits on conference realignment. Protections for the non-revenue Olympic sports that now exist — precariously — under the inescapable shadow of football. Would it all affect college sports in Idaho? Absolutely. And should you care about all of that, even if you don’t care about college sports? Also, absolutely. An athletic program isn’t an entity unto itself. Increasingly, colleges and universities are looking to athletics as a revenue generator. This isn’t new: athletic success has long equated to increases in applications, enrollment and donor support. Now, colleges and universities want to use their athletic facilities to rake in revenue, and not just on game day. They want their facilities to bring in concerts and corporate retreats and support lucrative on-campus development. That long game hinges on staying competitive on turf and hardwood. Which puts college athletics in the unnatural position of hoping Congress will come to the rescue. “We’re living insanity, and the fact that the federal government’s having to get involved at all, I think, tells that story,” Boise State University athletic director Jeramiah Dickey told EdNews Thursday. What happened in Congress, and what happens next Monday’s 77-22 Senate vote was noteworthy — especially considering how much the sponsors crammed into the Protect College Sports Act . Far from a do-nothing bill, it tries to solve all of college sports’ problems in one shot. One big change: The bill will allow a college to pay its student-athletes up to $49 million a year, shattering the current $21 million “revenue sharing” cap. That higher cap would apply to everyone — but practically speaking, it may only be an issue in the NCAA’s so-called “Power Four” conferences, the Big Ten, the Southeastern Conference, the Big XII and the Atlantic Coast Conference. Terry Gawlik University of Idaho athletic director Terry Gawlik doesn’t expect to see her Big Sky Conference brethren bumping up against a $49 million cap. “They can make the cap as high as they want it for the Power Four, but we’re never going to get to that level of paying student athletes,” she said this week. “So that’s not something that affects us daily.” But the $49 million cap could affect Boise State. The Broncos made the first 12-team College Football Playoff two years ago and are contenders again this year — and landing in the CFP will pit Boise State against big-money programs that could push up to the salary cap. (Boise State paid its student-athletes $10 million last budget year.) Dickey said he’s “not a huge fan” of the $49 million cap, but he’s glad to see the bill set some kind of maximum. Both Gawlik and Dickey like another key piece of the bill. It would allow student-athletes to transfer once in their college careers — and force repeat transfers to sit out a season. The limits on transfers will restore stability in the locker room, Gawlik said. In a related vein, Dickey likes the limited, five-year window for athletes to complete their playing careers. “This is a chapter,” he said. “This is not forever.” The bill also sidesteps a political minefield: state laws restricting transgender athletes. As Politico reported last month , co-sponsor Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, inserted language clarifying that the federal law would not supersede state bans on transgender athletes. For Gov. Brad Little, who signed the nation’s first transgender athletics ban into law in 2020 , that’s a non-negotiable, spokeswoman Emily Callihan said this week. “Gov. items.body: The Idaho Education Association (IEA) is cutting about 13% of its staff and closing its regional offices, leaders of the statewide teachers’ union announced this week. The cost-cutting measures come after union members told IEA’s board of directors to take a closer look at the organization’s budget and after a new law restricting taxpayer support for teachers’ union activities took effect. IEA is eliminating four union organizer positions, according to Executive Director Paul Stark. It’s also closing five regional offices, “centralizing operations in its Boise office.” And it’s turning Summer Institute, an annual professional development event, into an every-other-year event. IEA’s board of directors announced the cuts in an email to union members Monday. The board includes two dozen people, most of whom represent nine different geographic regions of the state. “Over the summer, we, your elected Board of Directors, carefully considered several options, asked difficult questions, and made decisions to put IEA on stronger financial footing for the future,” the board’s email said. “These decisions were not made lightly. They affect people. People who have dedicated themselves to serving our members and our profession.” Paul Stark, executive director of the Idaho Education Association " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-701x1180.jpg" class="wp-image-44392 size-thumbnail" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-119x200.jpg" alt="" width="119" height="200" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-119x200.jpg 119w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-368x620.jpg 368w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-701x1180.jpg 701w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-913x1536.jpg 913w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-1217x2048.jpg 1217w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-scaled.jpg 1521w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 119px) 100vw, 119px" /> Paul Stark, executive director of the Idaho Education Association The cuts followed a directive from IEA’s Delegate Assembly, a gathering of hundreds of local union leaders, the email said. In April the assembly told the board to “thoroughly examine” IEA’s budget and ensure that the union was “operating within its means.” The board also considered “the challenges created by recent legislative policies, including House Bill 516 ,” the email said. Enacted during this year’s legislative session , House Bill 516 prohibited public schools from using taxpayer-funded resources, such as payroll systems, to accommodate union activities. The Delegate Assembly issued a vote of no confidence in Gov. Brad Little for signing the “union-busting” bill into law. It took effect July 1. It’s unclear to what extent HB 516 factored into the downsizing. Among other restrictions, the law prohibits school districts from using payroll systems to deduct union dues. Districts also can’t offer teachers paid time off to engage in union activities unless IEA reimburses the district. And districts can’t give the union teachers’ contact information without their consent. The Freedom Foundation — an anti-union think tank based in Olympia, Wash. — for years lobbied lawmakers to enact the restrictions after it published a report arguing that Idaho unions were benefiting from government funds, facilities, resources and personnel. IEA leaders have repeatedly said that the union doesn’t receive taxpayer funding. But Stark didn’t provide specifics on how the law factored into the layoffs and office closures. “Idaho students and educators are only one month into the new school year, so the full effects of HB 516 on public education and the IEA have yet to be seen,” he said in an emailed statement Wednesday.

In an interview Tuesday, Berch attributed his fundraising success to engaging directly with voters and knocking on tens of thousands of doors in his legislative district. “It’s really very humbling, and it tells me that people like what I’m doing in terms of knocking on doors, holding in-person town hall meetings and sending out very detailed newsletters so they know the reason why I vote the way I do,” Berch said. Most of Berch’s campaign contributions came from people and from within Idaho. According to online state campaign finance reports, Berch raised $153,816 from people, $27,450 from companies, $9,000 from political committees and $1,000 from Democratic central committees. (Shelby Wyatt/Source NM) An Idaho judge dismissed a lawsuit from a Boise daycare and parents that sought to block enforcement of a state law that bans daycares from requiring vaccines or medical treatment. The lawsuit claimed that the Idaho Medical Freedom Act was unconstitutionally vague, arguing its language bans a range of routine health protections — including handwashing and sending home sick kids. But last week, Chief U.S. District Judge for the District of Idaho Amanda K. Brailsford granted Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s request to dismiss the lawsuit, which was brought by Le Soleil Child Care LLC, and three parents whose kids attend the daycare or hope to. In her ruling, the federal judge wrote she agreed with Labrador’s interpretation of the law’s definition of “medical interventions,” writing that they refer to health actions that are “medical in nature.” “The (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) plainly and unambiguously sets out a standard of prohibited conduct that gives a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited,” Brailsford wrote, ruling that the daycare didn’t show that the state law was unconstitutionally vague. “The Court agrees with the AG that Le Soleil is free to promote its beliefs and values about public health and vaccinations …” the judge wrote. “The only thing the (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) prevents is Le Soleil requiring that only vaccinated students hear those values.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE AG praises court ruling. Parents, daycare consider appealing, lawyer says. The ruling upholds a state law that bans daycares, businesses, governments and schools from mandating vaccines or “medical interventions,” which are defined as: “a medical procedure, treatment, device, drug injection, medication, or medical action taken to diagnose, prevent, or cure a disease or alter the health or biological function of a person.” In a statement, Labrador said he was pleased with the court’s decision. “Parents make medical decisions for their children. A daycare does not,” Labrador said in a statement . “The Legislature protected that choice in the Medical Freedom Act, and the court upheld it. Daycares can tell parents what they believe about vaccines and health, but they cannot turn a child away because of a parent’s medical decision. That decision belongs to families, and I’m pleased the court agreed.” Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? The state has reported 10 measles cases this year, as nearby states experience outbreaks. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle) A new data center campus could soon be coming to federal land near Hermiston in eastern Oregon. It would be the first in Oregon sited on federal public land, and one of at least 12 proposed for more than 17,500 Bureau of Land Management acres across western states under President Donald Trump’s July 2025 executive order to hasten data center development. The proposals on federal land in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming were first reported last week by The Washington Sun, whose reporters reviewed difficult to find right-of-way requests via BLM’s Mineral and Land Records System . The bulk of federally managed land in the U.S. is in the West, including in Oregon where half the state’s land is owned and managed by the federal government. Oregon is among the top 10 markets for data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research. Under the executive order, Trump mandated that federally owned land and resources be used for “the expeditious and orderly development of data centers (…) to be used in service of the prosperity and security of the American people.” It’s the first time the Bureau of Land Management, tasked with managing more than 245 million public acres for uses that include animal grazing, timber harvesting and recreation, has been ordered to include data centers in its portfolio. Several months after Trump issued the order, the California-based energy company Copia, which has an office in Lake Oswego, submitted an application to site the Charlestown Data Center and Battery Energy Storage System in Umatilla County on 106 acres of BLM land. items.body: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright (center) visits Idaho National Laboratory with Idaho Gov. Brad Little (right) in December 2025. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Wood/U.S. Department of Energy) Editor’s Note: This is the first installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining the proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focuses on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho. The series continues Monday and Tuesday with a closer look at the cases for and against bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Idaho Gov. Brad Little said he will not jeopardize the health of the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer or the health of Idahoans as he continues to negotiate potentially bringing a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. “I’ve had this direct conversation with Secretary (of Energy Chris) Wright: Disposal of spent fuel over the aquifer in Idaho – that’s a nonstarter,” Little said in an interview Wednesday at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. In July, U.S. Department of Energy officials announced that Idaho is one of five states selected as a finalist to host one of the new innovation campuses. Little signed a memorandum of understanding in July with the U.S. Department of Energy, or DOE, to hold formal discussions and negotiations about bringing an innovation campus to Idaho. The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer is outlined in orange of this map of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. (Map courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey) If Idaho is selected as a host site, the federal government has said the state will have to accept shipments of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste from other states. A Request for Information Response that Little signed and submitted to the federal government in March describes an accelerated process that takes “months rather than decades” to bring the “initial capabilities” of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus online in 2027. But on Wednesday, Little said things aren’t moving that quickly. “There’s a long way to go before this happens,” Little said. “(The DOE) would love to identify some sites, and I believe … they may need something by the end of the year. But it will not be in any way, shape or form a final agreement.” Little said the documents he signed do not obligate Idaho to host an innovation campus or accept nuclear fuel or radioactive waste. Instead, the agreements simply bring Idaho to the negotiating table, the governor said. Little said it makes sense for Idaho to be at the negotiating table because of the potential economic benefits to the state, the infrastructure, the experience at Idaho National Laboratory in eastern Idaho and the need for additional, reliable energy. The memorandum of understanding lists a Sept. 30 deadline, but Little said he doesn’t think agreements will be reached that quickly, and he suggested the two sides could either continue talks or sign another memorandum of understanding with a later deadline. Officials at Idaho National Laboratory declined to comment for this series of articles. What is a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus? There are now five other potential host sites for one or more DOE innovation campuses – Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and West Virginia. According to the DOE , a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus is “designed to support activities across the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel and final disposition of used nuclear fuel.
